asanas.name: Padmasana
asanas.about: The classic seat for meditation: each foot rests on the opposite thigh, soles turned up, knees on the ground. It locks the base and holds the spine upright with little effort once the hips are open enough.
benefits: Very stable base; the body can stay still for long sittings
Encourages an upright spine and a steady, even breath
Traditionally said to settle the mind and support prāṇāyāma
asanas.caution: Needs open hips. Never force the knees; if they lift or hurt, use Ardha Padmasana or Siddhasana instead.

steps.text: Sit on a folded blanket with both legs extended and the spine tall.
Bend the right knee and place the right foot on the left thigh, sole up, heel close to the navel.
Bend the left knee and lift the left foot onto the right thigh, sole up.
Rest the hands in your chosen mudra, lengthen the spine and relax the shoulders.

asanas.name: Ardha Padmasana
asanas.about: One foot rests on the opposite thigh while the other tucks beneath the knee. A gentler version of the lotus that keeps most of its stability.
benefits: Stable and upright with less demand on the hips and knees
A step toward full Padmasana
Comfortable for medium-length sittings
asanas.caution: Alternate which leg is on top between sessions to keep the hips even. Avoid if the knee of the top leg strains.

steps.text: Sit with both legs extended and the spine tall.
Bend the left knee and tuck the left foot under the right thigh.
Bend the right knee and place the right foot on the left thigh, sole up.
Settle both knees toward the floor, rest the hands in your mudra and lengthen the spine.

asanas.name: Siddhasana
asanas.about: One heel presses at the perineum and the other heel rests just above it, the feet tucked between calf and thigh. Haṭha texts rank it among the foremost seats for meditation.
benefits: Firm, symmetrical base with the spine naturally erect
Less hip rotation than Padmasana for many people
Haṭha tradition associates the heel placement with steadying the lower centres (Muladhara)
asanas.caution: Avoid pressing hard on the perineum; keep the pressure gentle. Not advised with sciatica or recent groin injury without guidance.

steps.text: Sit with both legs extended.
Bend the left knee and draw the left heel in to rest gently at the perineum.
Bend the right knee and place the right heel just above the left, tucking the toes between calf and thigh.
Rest the hands in your mudra, keep the spine tall and the chin slightly drawn in.

asanas.name: Vajrasana
asanas.about: Kneeling with the knees together and sitting back on the heels. The simplest upright seat and a good choice when cross-legged postures are uncomfortable.
benefits: Keeps the spine upright with almost no hip flexibility needed
Traditionally practised after meals as it is said to aid digestion
Easy to enter and leave
asanas.caution: Use a cushion between heels and buttocks if the knees or ankles complain. Avoid with knee injuries.

steps.text: Kneel on a soft mat with the knees together and the tops of the feet on the floor.
Bring the big toes together, let the heels part slightly and sit back between them.
Rest the hands in your mudra on the thighs or in the lap, and lengthen the spine.

mudras.name: Jnana Mudra
mudras.about: The tip of the index finger touches the tip of the thumb; the other three fingers stay relaxed and extended. The hands rest on the knees, palms facing down.
benefits: A calm, grounded hand position for long sittings
Palms down is traditionally described as introverting and settling
Keeps the arms relaxed and the shoulders even

steps.text: Rest the hands on the knees, palms down, fingers relaxed.
Curl each index finger toward the thumb.
Touch the index fingertip to the thumb tip, forming a circle; keep the other three fingers extended.

mudras.name: Chin Mudra
mudras.about: The same finger seal as Jnana Mudra, with the palms turned up on the knees.
benefits: Palms up is traditionally described as open and receptive
A light, uplifting variation of Jnana Mudra
Comfortable for breath-focused practice

steps.text: Rest the backs of the hands on the knees, palms facing up.
Curl each index finger toward the thumb.
Touch the index fingertip to the thumb tip, forming a circle; let the other three fingers extend softly.

mudras.name: Dhyana Mudra
mudras.about: The hands rest in the lap, palms up, the right hand on top of the left, and the thumb tips touch lightly to form an oval.
benefits: Gathers attention to the centre of the body
Supports a soft, steady posture for long meditation
The touching thumbs give quick feedback when attention drifts

steps.text: Bring both hands to the lap, palms up, just below the navel.
Rest the right hand on the left, fingers overlapping.
Let the thumb tips meet lightly above the palms, forming an oval.

mudras.name: Bhairava Mudra
mudras.about: The right hand rests in the left in the lap, both palms up, thumbs relaxed. (With the left hand on top it is called Bhairavi Mudra.)
benefits: A simple, restful hand position
Balances both sides of the body in the lap
Easy to hold for long sittings

steps.text: Bring both hands into the lap, palms up.
Place the right hand in the left palm and let the thumbs relax.

mudras.name: Yoni Mudra
mudras.about: The fingers interlace; the index fingertips touch pointing down and the thumb tips touch pointing up, forming a diamond held at the lower abdomen. (Some Haṭha texts use the same name for the sense-closing practice also called Shanmukhi Mudra; this is the hand-seal form.)
benefits: Turns attention inward, toward the lower centres
Joins both hands symmetrically at the body's centre
Often used before or during quiet breathing

steps.text: Bring the palms together in front of the lower abdomen.
Interlace the middle, ring and little fingers.
Touch the index fingertips pointing down and the thumb tips pointing up, forming a diamond.

mudras.name: Anjali Mudra
mudras.about: The palms press together in front of the heart, fingers pointing up. Used to begin and end practice, and for prayer or chanting.
benefits: Centres attention at the heart (Anahata)
Brings left and right sides together
A natural gesture of respect to begin a session

steps.text: Bring the hands up in front of the chest.
Press the palms together evenly, thumbs lightly touching the sternum.

mudras.name: Prana Mudra
mudras.about: The tips of the ring and little fingers touch the tip of the thumb; the index and middle fingers stay extended. The hands rest on the knees, palms up.
benefits: Traditionally associated with vitality and the energy of Prana
A steady, relaxed hand position
Often paired with breath awareness

steps.text: Rest the hands on the knees, palms up.
Curl the ring and little fingers toward the thumb.
Touch the ring and little fingertips to the thumb tip; keep the index and middle fingers extended.

mudras.name: Vayu Mudra
mudras.about: The index finger folds down so its tip rests at the base of the thumb, and the thumb presses lightly over the folded index finger. The other three fingers stay extended. The hands rest on the knees, palms up.
benefits: Traditionally used to settle restlessness and an overactive mind
Associated in mudra practice with balancing the air (vāyu) element
A steady, grounding hand position for seated breathing
mudras.caution: Press gently; release if the hand or thumb tires. Traditionally practised for limited periods (about 15–45 minutes).

steps.text: Rest the hands on the knees, palms up, fingers relaxed.
Fold each index finger down so its tip touches the base of the thumb.
Press the thumb gently over the folded index finger; keep the other fingers extended.

mudras.name: Shambhavi Mudra
mudras.about: A gaze rather than a hand seal: the eyes look gently up and inward toward the eyebrow centre (Ajna). The hands usually rest in Jnana or Chin Mudra on the knees.
benefits: Directs attention to Ajna, the eyebrow centre
Steadies the gaze and, with it, the mind
Described in Haṭha texts as a powerful aid to concentration
mudras.caution: Hold only briefly at first and release at any eye strain; relax the eyes between rounds.

steps.text: Sit steadily with the hands in Jnana Mudra; close the eyes and relax the face.
Open the eyes softly and look straight ahead.
Without moving the head, raise the gaze up and inward toward the eyebrow centre.
After a few breaths, release the gaze and close the eyes.
